name: Rosa Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal site day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I frame new houses, from walls through joists and roof trusses. I have a trade certificate and years of experience, so the best part is seeing a roof line come out straight after a wet week. I am not the quickest on the ladder now, but I know the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the site like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Karl, my husband, stopped his old trade last year, and our children are grown. We own our house, have more than six months saved and have talked about when I might stop roofing. My pay is high for a carpenter; I have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the framing crew that a small office shortcut does not change a crooked slab. We still need hands to lift trusses and eyes to check the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karl and I have the house paid and more than six months saved. My wages are good for this trade and there are plenty of nearby builders, so I can see a way to stop working on our planned date if our accounts keep behaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing houses and measuring roof lines with my crew. I would leave the office software to the clerk and keep making the same savings transfer from wages, with no new gadget to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My knees are the thing I think about on a frosty roof. A computer in the site office does not bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before the planned date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A serious knee problem might, but we would check the household accounts first. I am not counting on an automatic payment at any particular age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new office tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and the plans and tape measure already tell me what I need on the roof.

say: I would tell the crew **trusses and roof lines** still need workers on site.
I would accept small **office savings** without changing my measuring routine.
think: Our **paid house and savings** make the current retirement discussion possible.
My **knees** are a more immediate risk than limited AI.
do: Keep **house framing** and checking roof lines by hand.
Maintain the existing **monthly savings** transfer without starting new software.
feel: **Calm** about pay, with ordinary concern about knees.
S0.quote: My knees are the thing I think about on a frosty roof.
fieldNote: Her strong cushion, high pay and many nearby builders support a **secure baseline** for retirement planning.
She has never used AI and prefers a **familiar site routine**.

steps.text: Keep framing houses and checking roof lines with the crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the builder a computer can buy timber, but the frame still has to meet the actual slab. I would want a working carpenter checking the new cut lists before lumber is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may shrink, and faster schedules could send crews between sites with less paid waiting time. I could lose some travel pay, though Karl no longer needs a wage and our savings would cover a lean spell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare two monthly rosters with my pay slips and ask the foreman to keep a named carpenter on each cut list. If travel pay falls, Karl and I would postpone replacing the garden fence until we see the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible smaller pay packet, even though the house is secure. I have no appetite for doing office checks on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the carpenter check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the slab is square and whether the timber lengths fit the site measurement. A computer can order a perfect wall for the wrong foundation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another nearby builder now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There are plenty of jobs, but I would wait for a real pay change and a posted offer before leaving a crew I know.

say: I would insist a **working carpenter** checks AI cut lists against the real slab.
I would ask for **named sign-off** before timber orders leave the office.
think: My **travel pay** could shrink under tighter schedules.
Our **savings and paid house** protect us, but I would still notice lost wages.
do: Compare two **rosters and pay slips** for lost travel pay.
Delay the **garden fence** if travel pay falls until the next contract is clear.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic pay cut despite a safe home.
S1.quote: A computer can order a perfect wall for the wrong foundation.
fieldNote: The threatened income is **travel pay**, not an immediate end to hands-on framing.
Her spending decision waits for **measured lost pay** and a clearer next contract.

steps.text: Delay garden fence replacement only if travel pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 can plan a roof but cannot nail the trusses. Around 2031 a capable robot may do it, and I would want a trial on a real uneven house before trusting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three when robots arrive, about a year past the date Karl and I hope I can finish if our accounts allow. The office change might still cut my paid days before then, so I cannot simply ignore the fast timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking framing shifts and review our retirement figures with Karl this winter. If two rosters show fewer paid days before our planned date, I would apply to posted nearby carpentry work only if its firm pay covers the remaining household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the last good earning years, with enough savings to plan. I am not retiring on a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward to 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I want to leave on the date we already discussed if health and accounts permit. A figure check is preparation, not an exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the robot trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A roof on a slab that is not quite square, with the machine stopped before a worker enters its path. I would not let anyone trial it over an occupied room.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** plans roofs before capable robots reach trusses around 2031.
I would insist on a **real uneven-house trial** before crews are cut.
think: My planned exit may precede **2031 robots** if health and accounts allow.
A faster office change could still cut my **paid days** before that exit.
do: Keep **paid framing shifts** while available and review household figures with Karl.
Apply to **posted nearby carpentry jobs** after two reduced rosters only for firm household-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost earnings near retirement, with savings to respond.
S2.quote: I am not retiring on a headline.
fieldNote: Her retirement is conditional on **real accounts and health**, not guaranteed by age.
The job search needs **two reduced rosters** and a posted firm-pay role.

steps.text: Keep paid framing shifts while available and check household figures
Apply to posted nearby carpentry jobs after two reduced rosters for firm household-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew five years is enough to test framing robots without putting anyone underneath a moving truss. A builder should start with the machine isolated and a crew member able to call stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may rewrite the cutting lists, but capable robots arrive around 2034. I would be sixty six by then and hope to have left regular roofs if Karl and I can afford it, so my own income looks safer than in the fast case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing through the next year and show the younger carpenter how I set roof lines. Karl and I would review our savings each autumn, and if I am still employed in 2034 I would take only safe paid shifts that my knees can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the near years. The apprentices have longer to face the machine than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave sooner because of the 2034 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have an existing target and will check savings and health against it. A robot arriving later does not make me rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who calls stop in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The carpenter watching the truss path. Nobody should have to ask the office for permission to stop a dangerous lift.

say: I would require **isolated-machine trials** before 2034 framing robots lift trusses.
I would teach the next carpenter **roof-line checks** while there is time.
think: I hope to leave regular roofs before **2034**, conditional on savings and health.
The **2031 cutting-list change** is smaller than the later hands-on robot change.
do: Keep **roof framing** next year and teach line setting to a younger carpenter.
Review **retirement savings** with Karl each autumn before settling an exit.
feel: **Calm** about near-term earnings, concerned for younger carpenters.
S3.quote: Nobody should have to ask the office for permission to stop a dangerous lift.
fieldNote: She uses the extra years for **hands-on teaching**, not a speculative technology course.
The possible exit before robots remains **conditional**, and 2034 work is explicitly limited if she remains employed.

steps.text: Keep framing roofs next year and teach younger carpenter line checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices they can learn the whole framing trade before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would make them measure a roof twice before trusting a generated list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy one when robots follow. If Karl and I can fund the date we have been discussing, I expect to have stopped roof work before either one; if not, I would still need some paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the house framing rota in 2026 and check our accounts with Karl at year end. In the first year after 2036, if retired as planned, I would not book roof shifts; if still working, I would take only paid ground-level tasks my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machines, uneasy about whether my knees and our savings line up. There is time to put the tools down properly if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is this an earlier retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Karl and I are still testing the date we already had in mind against actual expenses. The card has not moved it forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentice on the last roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark the line with a pencil, then check the timber before lifting it. A clean drawing is no comfort after a bad cut.

say: I would protect **full apprenticeship time** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots change framing.
I would keep **physical measurements** in site training.
think: I expect to have left roofs before **2036** only if savings and health allow.
If not retired, I may need **paid ground work** as my knees age.
do: Keep the **2026 framing rota** and check accounts with Karl at year end.
After **2036**, take only manageable paid ground tasks if still employed.
feel: **Uneasy** about health and retirement funding, with no near-term AI pay threat.
S4.quote: A clean drawing is no comfort after a bad cut.
fieldNote: She separates 2026 work from **conditional post-2036 employment**.
The existing retirement target depends on **accounts and knees**, with no implied early exit or guaranteed payment.

steps.text: Keep 2026 house framing shifts while knees allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because office changes might cut my last paid roofing years before I can afford to stop. A written roster plan and firm nearby carpentry offers would help Karl and me judge our options.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop a truss robot when a carpenter is in its path. A safe roof starts with someone willing to halt the lift.

headlineQuote: A safe roof starts with someone willing to halt the lift.
portrait: **Rosa**, 58, is an experienced house framer with a trade certificate, high pay, a paid home and substantial savings.
Her husband has left his old trade, their children are grown and **many nearby builders** offer alternative work.
She has never used **AI tools**, trusts measurement and treats retirement as conditional on savings and her knees.
The **2028 case** concerns her most because paid roof work could shrink before the retirement date she hopes to afford.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her final paid roofing years before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A written **roster plan** and firm nearby offers would help her decide.
